chunks.text: 2 Method Our method effectively segments multi-channel noisy images using only a few sparse scribbles denoting nuclei or whole-cell (nucleus + surrounding cytoplasm and membrane compartments) segmentations. We assume that annotators provides annotations indicating foreground regions (e.g., a line inside a cell) and background regions (e.g., rough boundary surrounding the cell). Given the variability in image size and scale across acquisitions, we employ a U-net architecture to develop a space-preserving segmentation and classification network. We assume that the background and the target biological instances can be approximated as a mixture of distributions. This assumption introduces a level of quantization to the denoised image, with the resulting reconstruction loss serving to improve the segmentation objective. Assume that we have a dataset containing N N pairs of noisy images and scribbles { x n , y n } n = 1 N \{x^{n},y^{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} . Here x ∈ ℝ W × H x\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times H} is a noisy input image and y ∈ { 0 , 1 } W × H × 2 y\in\{0,1\}^{W\times H\times 2} is the corresponding ground truth scribble per-pixel, indicating if a pixel belongs to background (boundaries) or foreground (i.e. cell instance). For notational compactness, we use the sub-index i i to refer to the spatial location of a pixel instead of 2-coordinate location ( i , j ) (i,j) ; we also overload the scribble notation y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } 2 y_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{2} where y i y_{i} sometimes satisfies ‖ y i ‖ 1 = 1 ||y_{i}||_{1}=1 (one-hot class encoding where scribbles are present), but otherwise satisfies ‖ y i ‖ 1 = 0 ||y_{i}||_{1}=0 to indicate no scribble is present. Since we consider a low-data regime, we sample a set of B B image-scribble pair patches of size 128 × 128 128\times 128 , denoted as { x b , y b } b ∈ B \{x^{b},y^{b}\}_{b\in B} , from the available N N pairs, creating a total of N ∗ B N*B patches for training.

Validation patches are drawn from the same training set, ensuring minimal overlap with the training patches. Figure 1 : Overview of ImPartial training pipeline on multiplex data. Following the blind-spot network proposed in Noise2Void [ 6 ] , for each image patch x b x^{b} in our training set of patches b ∈ B b\in B , we generate a partial copy x ¯ b \bar{x}^{b} , where a random set of pixels I b I_{b} is substituted by random values in the vicinity ( I b = { i : x ¯ i b ← x j ​ ( i ) b , j ​ ( i ) ≠ i } I_{b}=\{i:\bar{x}^{b}_{i}\leftarrow x^{b}_{j(i)},j(i)\neq i\} ) i.e. the blind spot patch, x ¯ b \bar{x}^{b} , assigns random local values to pixel locations in I b I_{b} while preserving original values elsewhere. The imputation patch I b I_{b} is a mask with nonzero values only at imputed pixel locations, sampled at a probability of 0.2. Reconstruction Loss using Gaussian Mixtures. We model the intensity of a multi-channel image as a mixture of M M components ( m = 1 m=1 to M M in Eq. 1), grouped into K K disjoint subsets corresponding to different classes (e.g., background and foreground nuclei, so K = 2 K=2 ). This results in M = ∑ k = 0 K − 1 | m k | M=\sum^{K-1}_{k=0}|m_{k}| , where m k m_{k} represents the subset of mixture components modeling the intensity of pixels in class k k . The sum of mixture components for class k k , ∑ m ∈ m k ρ θ , i m ​ ( x ¯ b ) \sum_{m\in m_{k}}\rho^{m}_{\theta,i}(\bar{x}^{b}) , corresponds directly to its probability. The mixture reconstruction loss is back propagated exclusively for imputed pixels I b I_{b} , preventing the network from learning the identity.

The dual perspective is that we encourage our recovered class labels to be consistent with the reconstruction objective defined for the mixture loss. Joint loss. We combine the quantization reconstruction mixture loss and the scribble segmentation loss that makes use of the available scribbles into a single training loss. Extension to multiple channels. We extend the framework to multiple channels (input image x ∈ ℝ W × H × C x\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times H\times C} ) in the natural way by computing the mixture (quantization) statistics jointly across all channels C C . Across all experiments, each component M M in the mixture is modeled as a fixed-variance Gaussian with mean τ m ∈ ℝ C \tau^{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} . The component mask ρ θ m ​ ( ⋅ ) \rho^{m}_{\theta}(\cdot) is therefore shared across channels. Since we assume the scribbled mask is related to objects that appear as foreground components on at least one channel, we can still compute the scribble mask by summing over the foreground components of the multi-channel mixture mask. The joint loss therefore remains unchanged. 3 Results and Discussion We compared ImPartial with SOTA algorithms on three widely used, expert-annotated public datasets for multiplexed imaging. The ground truth annotations were randomly sampled to generate the required scribbles. TissueNet. This is a 2-channel dataset [ 4 ] containing a nuclear (e.g.

DAPI) and a cytoplasmic or membrane marker (e.g. Pan-Keratin). It is collected from different imaging platforms and contains different tissue types and disease states. We used the originally released TissueNet 1.0 dataset with their train/test splits: train - 2600 (512x512), test - 1250 (256x256). CPDMFCI. This dataset [ 1 ] includes annotations on multiplex images from three fluorescent imaging platforms and over 40 antibody markers, offering both whole-cell and nuclear annotations for granular segmentation of cellular compartments. To accommodate platform differences, annotations span tissues acquired through sequential immunofluorescence with unmixing (Akoya Vectra 3.0), sequential IF with narrowband capture (Ultivue InSituPlex with Zeiss Axioscan), and cyclical IF with narrowband capture (Akoya CODEX). We selected 81 images (66 train, 15 test) as 400×400 pixel crops from the larger multiplex image set. See results in Fig. 3 , note that existing methods do not support 3+ channels. IHC. The publicly available DeepLIIF dataset [ 3 ] , which consists of co-registered images of IHC, hematoxylin, and multiplex immunofluorescence (mpIF) channels (DAPI, Lap2, and Ki67) acquired from lung and bladder tissue sections. All slides were scanned using a ZEISS Axioscan system.

The multi-modal images were preprocessed through scaling and affine co-registration to the corresponding fixed IHC images (512 × 512), 1,975 images were used for training and 391 images testing. Evaluation Metrics. For quantitative evaluation and comparison with other methods, we compute Instance Segmentation metrics such as mean intersection over union (mIOU), Average Precision (AP), F1-score at 0.5 IoU threshold as implemented in the Stardist [ 10 ] and Cellpose [ 8 ] libraries. Ablation Study. We performed an ablation study by first removing the scribble loss followed by removal of the reconstruction loss Table 2 .

When the scribble loss is removed, the method defaults to Noise2Void [ 6 ] and in that case, it is difficult for the model to separate touching or overlapping cells. For the latter case where we removed the reconstruction loss, we show that the method struggles on TissueNet images, especially the ones acquired from the MIBI platform, which tend to have significant noise in the background. These results show that using both loss functions is necessary to obtain optimal results. Table 2 : Ablation study analysis on TN dataset with 10% scribbles. We use a U-Net with depth 4 4 , 64 64 initial feature maps, and convolution kernel size of 3 3 . We use a batch size of size 64 64 , trained for 200 200 epochs and Adam optimizer method with learning rate 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} , stopping criteria was based on validation performance on the joint training loss.

For modeling the cluster components as fixed-variance Gaussian distributions with parametric mean, we used a total of M=4 clusters, 2 each modeling the background and foreground. All the experiments reported in the paper were run for single iteration using 3 different seeds, the standard deviation was < < 0.006 across all metrics. Acknowledgments.
